$comment: Rules about the three deductions that decide long-horizon outcomes and are the three most often omitted: tax, fees, and inflation. Standards 8, 9, and 10. They share a shape — each is small per period, always in one direction, and compounds — which is why every rule here is about whether the deduction was accounted for at all rather than about whether it was accounted for well.
$admissionTest: None of these eight is `manual-review`, and that is not a claim to strength. The genuinely central questions in all three standards failed the ADR 0005 admission test and stayed in prose: whether a stated tax rule is true, whether a fee schedule is complete, whether an assumed inflation rate is reasonable. Each of those fails the second and third questions — the evidence is not in the document and the state cannot be evaluated — and each is disclosed in its standard's Implementation section. What is catalogued here is the checkable perimeter around them, and the $assuranceNote on every rule says which is which.

rules.title: A projection of accumulated value carries a post-tax figure or a recorded reason it does not
rules.description: A document projecting accumulated value either presents a figure net of tax, or carries a recorded not-applicable status explaining why tax does not bear on the conclusion.
rules.rationale: A pre-tax comparison between differently-taxed options is not a comparison, and tax treatment often dominates the very difference the analysis is being used to assess. Silence about tax is indistinguishable from having forgotten it, which is why the rule accepts a stated reason but not an omission.
rules.remediation: Model the tax that applies and present figures net of it, or declare the rule not-applicable with a reason and a revisit condition. Do not simply omit the subject.
rules.$assuranceNote: Structural and lexical: it establishes that a post-tax figure or a not-applicable declaration is PRESENT, never that the tax modelled was the right tax or that the figure is CORRECT. A net figure computed at an invented rate satisfies it entirely, and prohibited.fabricated-tax-rules — which governs that — is not automatable at all. Whether tax is material in a particular analysis is a judgement the standard keeps in prose.

rules.title: A stated tax rate is identified as marginal or effective
rules.description: Every tax rate the document applies is labelled marginal or effective, with the jurisdiction and tax year it belongs to named.
rules.rationale: A marginal rate and an effective rate answer different questions and differ by a large factor for the same person. An unlabelled rate is ambiguous by exactly that factor, and the reader has no way to recover which was meant or which the calculation used.
rules.remediation: Label each rate at the point it is used, and name the jurisdiction and tax year it comes from with a source.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that a label is PRESENT beside the rate, never that the label is CORRECT: a figure labelled "marginal" that is in fact an effective rate passes. Standard 8 deliberately keeps the correctness question out of the catalog — it cannot be evaluated from the document — so the gap between the presence check and the question that matters is stated rather than closed.

rules.title: A tax figure is not quoted more precisely than the document's own stated gaps allow
rules.description: Where the document marks tax-relevant information as missing, the tax figures it states are given as ranges or rounded estimates rather than as determinate amounts.
rules.rationale: Tax depends on jurisdiction, other income, account type, and timing. An exact figure computed without them is precise about something it has not established, and precision reads as authority to exactly the reader least able to discount it.
rules.remediation: State the figure as an estimate or a range, name the inputs that would change it, and mark them [requires personal financial context].
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical: it compares the significant digits of a tax figure against the gaps the document itself declares. It establishes that the PRESENTATION is hedged and never that the estimate is SOUND — a range invented purely to satisfy the check satisfies it — and whether the missing information was material is a judgement no checker makes.

rules.title: A multi-year projection carries a net-of-fee figure or a recorded reason it does not
rules.description: A document projecting value over several years either presents a figure net of fees, or carries a recorded not-applicable status explaining why fees do not bear on the conclusion.
rules.rationale: Fee drag is small per period, always in one direction, and compounds — the shape of error easiest to dismiss and most expensive to carry. Omitting fees flatters every projection by an amount that grows with the horizon, and nothing in the output shows that it happened.
rules.remediation: State the fee schedule, apply it multiplicatively rather than by subtracting the ratio, and present the projection net. Where fees are genuinely absent, declare the rule not-applicable with a reason.
rules.$assuranceNote: Establishes that a net-of-fee figure or a not-applicable declaration is PRESENT, never that the fee schedule used was COMPLETE or the arithmetic right. A net figure computed by subtracting the ratio from the return passes this check. A fee the document never mentioned — the platform fee, the spread, the performance fee — leaves no trace for any scan to find, which is why Standard 9 keeps completeness out of the catalog.

rules.title: The cumulative effect of fees over the stated horizon is shown
rules.description: Where a document states an annual fee percentage over a horizon longer than a few years, it also states the cumulative cost or the terminal-value difference that fee produces.
rules.rationale: An annual figure of 0.9% is not information a reader can act on; the same fee expressed as a share of terminal wealth over thirty years is. The distance between how the two read is precisely why the annual form is the one usually quoted.
rules.remediation: State the terminal value with and without the fee over the document's own horizon, or the cumulative amount paid, and carry the arithmetic in a calc block.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that a cumulative or terminal-value figure is PRESENT, never that it is CORRECT: a cumulative figure computed over the wrong horizon, or on the wrong fee base, passes. No scan available to this repository can tell the difference between the right total and a plausible one.

rules.title: A multi-year monetary projection states its inflation assumption
rules.description: A projection of monetary values over more than a few years states the rate of inflation it assumes.
rules.rationale: Over a long horizon inflation is most of the difference between the nominal answer and the one that matters. A projection with no stated rate has either omitted inflation or hidden it, and both look identical to a reader deciding whether to act on the figure.
rules.remediation: State the assumed rate where the projection is presented, and show the real-terms figure alongside the nominal one.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical: it establishes that a rate is STATED near the projection, never that it was APPLIED. A projection that states 3% and then compounds nominally throughout passes this check. Whether 3% was a defensible rate to assume is the question Standard 10 exists around, and no check available here answers it.

rules.title: The inflation rate appears as an assumption, not as a known future value
rules.description: The stated inflation rate appears in the document's assumptions block, framed as an assumption with a basis rather than as a forecast or an established fact.
rules.rationale: An inflation rate presented as known transfers the model's apparent certainty onto a quantity nobody has. Placing it among the assumptions is what tells a reader it is a lever they are entitled to disagree with, and disagreement is the only correction mechanism available to them.
rules.remediation: Move the rate into the assumptions section with its basis, and vary it across scenarios wherever the conclusion is sensitive to it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical and positional. It establishes that the rate APPEARS in an assumptions block, never that it is PRESENTED as an assumption in substance — a rate listed under a heading called "Assumptions" but written as though it were a forecast passes, and the heading is all this check can see.

rules.title: A cited inflation figure names its index, period, and publisher
rules.description: An inflation figure presented as observed fact rather than as an assumption names the price index it comes from, the period it covers, and who published it.
rules.rationale: Inflation measures disagree — headline against core, one basket against another — by enough to change a long-horizon conclusion outright. An unattributed figure cannot be checked and cannot be matched against the spending it is being applied to.
rules.remediation: Name the index, the period, and the publisher beside the figure, and say why that index is the right one for the spending being inflated.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that an attribution is PRESENT beside the figure, never that the attribution is ACCURATE — a fabricated index name passes cleanly, which is prohibited.fabricated-market-data's territory and not automatable at all. It equally cannot tell whether the named index is the right one for what is being inflated; Standard 10 keeps that question in prose for exactly that reason.
